# Scintille

> Scintille is a cinematic 3D globe showing lightning across the planet in near real time, built on open satellite data. Flash brightness reflects the optical energy measured by the satellite, coverage gaps are shown rather than hidden, and every data source is attributed.

Scintille is live and public at https://scintille.app.

Lightning data comes from geostationary lightning imagers, which detect the optical pulses of lightning flashes from orbit, day and night:

- NOAA GOES Geostationary Lightning Mapper (GLM), on the GOES-East and GOES-West satellites, covering the Americas and the surrounding oceans.
- EUMETSAT Meteosat Third Generation (MTG) Lightning Imager, covering Europe, Africa and most of the Atlantic Ocean.

Asia, Oceania and the poles have no lightning feed yet and are shaded. Over Asia and Oceania, soft glows mark storm tops colder than 215 K in Himawari's hourly infrared: storms, not flashes, and many over the ocean have none. An empty region is not a region without lightning.

What you can do on the globe:

- Watch lightning live, about 70 seconds behind real time (Europe and Africa about 12 minutes behind).
- See hourly clouds, in relief from their cloud-top heights.
- Follow storms: flashes are grouped into storms, tracked, ranked and named. Storms can be followed while active and the strongest ones replayed for 60 days.
- Travel in time through the last three weeks of lightning, hour by hour.

Update cadence: the live feed publishes about every 20 seconds, clouds and storm tops every hour, the storm catalog every hour. Static pages are rebuilt when the site is deployed.

## Pages

- [Home](https://scintille.app/): the live lightning globe.
- [Status](https://scintille.app/status/): live health of the feed (throughput, latency, completeness, freshness, lakehouse and storms).
- [Methodology](https://scintille.app/methodology/): sources, live pipeline, lakehouse, storm catalog, stack, storage, coverage, limits and credits.
- [Privacy](https://scintille.app/privacy/): what the site collects (no cookies, anonymous visit counts).

## Data sources

- [NOAA GOES-R Geostationary Lightning Mapper](https://www.goes-r.gov/spacesegment/glm.html): lightning mapper on the GOES-East and GOES-West satellites.
- [EUMETSAT Meteosat Third Generation](https://www.eumetsat.int/meteosat-third-generation): satellite programme carrying the MTG Lightning Imager.
- Clouds: hourly composite of the NOAA GOES-East and GOES-West, JMA Himawari-9 (via NOAA) and EUMETSAT MTG full disks, gaps filled by NOAA NESDIS GMGSI. Cloud-top heights come from the infrared and the GFS temperature profile.
- Storm tops over Asia and Oceania: Himawari-9 infrared, the same frames as the clouds.
